3. The plaintiff’s case, in brief, was that the jote in question originally belonged to Kanak and Saraju Bala, each having 4 annas interest and Basanta Kumari, Sudhir Kumar, Provahati and Snehalata having 2 annas share each, in the said jote. Saraju Bala sold her share to pre-emptor-respondents No. 1-4 by a kabala dated 2-3-1953 and their names were recorded in S.A. Khatian No. 290. Kanak, Sudhir and Snehalata jointly sold their share to respondent No.5 Azizur Rahman Mia and the same has been recorded in S.A Khatian No. 291. Azizur Rahman transferred his purchased interest to the appellants by kabala dated 21-3-73 without notice to respondents No.1 to 4 who came to know of the same for the first time in Kartick, 1381 B.S. from Afazuddin Molla, father of the appellants and after obtaining certified copy of the registered kabala from Sub-Registrar's Office, Rajshahi on 22-11-74 they filed this pre-emption case on 6-12-74 after making necessary deposit. 

 4. It was asserted in the application for pre-emption that the land purchased by the pre-emptors from Saraju Bala had been re-corded in khatian no. 290 and the land purchased by Azizur Rahman had been recorded in khatian No. 291. 

 Leave was granted in the following terms:-"Mr. Jamiruddin Sircer, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner contends that the lower appellate Court reversed the decision of the trial Court without consideration of the documents on record particularly original C.S. Khatian Exts. C and C(1) Dakhilas Ext. B series. He argues that the lower appellate Court, as the last court of fact was under a legal duty to consider the entire evidence before reversing the decision of the trial court and that the High Court Division committed an error in not interfering with the decision of the lower appellate court in the aforesaid circumstances. The contention merits consideration." 

 10. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, the learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant argues that the High Court Division erred in failing to consider that the judgment of the lower appellate Court was not a proper judgment of reversal and that the finding of fact arrived at by the said Court was not on consideration of evidence. He, submits that the lower appellate Court did not at all consider the documentary evidence adduced by the appellants particularly C.S. Khatian Exts. C and C (1) and dakhilas Ext. B series. The learned Counsel further argues that the lower appellate Court was not correct in holding that there was absolutely no legal evidence about the spliting up of the original holding. 

 11. Mr. Shamsul Hoque Chowdhury, the learned Counsel, appearing for some of the respondents, however, argues that the learned Judge of the High Court Division in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure rightly refused to interfere with the finding of fact arrived at by the lower appellate Court, as regards the co-share ship and contiguous ownership of the pre-emptors. He further argues that Exts. C and C (1) relates to recording of separate khatian and jama under the Bengal Tenancy Act in the name of Azizur Rahman and the said exhibits are, therefore, not proof of separation of jama under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the lower appellate Court correctly held that there was no legal evidence about splitting up of the holding. 

 12. The trial Court held that the appellants (0.P. in the trial Court) filed C.S. Khatian No.144 being the original khatian and C.S. Khatian No. 144/2 and hal khatian 291, Exts. C and C (1) respectively showing recording of a separate khatian and separate jote and jama under B.T. Act in the name of Azizur Rahman creating separate jama. It was further held that Dakhilas Ext. B series also support the contention that jama of Azizur Rahman was separated from his time and rent was paid exclusively by him for his purchased portion. The aforesaid khatians were prepared before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force, by an order passed by a competent revenue officer and the order was given effect to by the co-sharers of the holding who paid rents and as such the holding stood separated under the law. So even if the order was not passed under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act such order cannot be overlooked in deciding a pre-emption petition under section 96 of the said Act. The pre-emptors prayed for pre-emption in 3 schedules Ka, Kha and Ga out of which admittedly they were not co-sharers as regards Kha and Ga schedules. On the basis of Exts. C and C (1) the trial Court found that the pre-emptors were not co-sharers to Ka schedule land.
